analysis.one_liner: Replaces the gridlocked Federal Election Commission with a smaller, independent enforcement agency for campaign finance laws.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration on June 22, 2006, and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, without a single vote in either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have abolished the Federal Election Commission, the six-member agency that enforces campaign finance laws, and replaced it with a three-member Federal Election Administration. The new agency would be an independent establishment whose three members could not share a political party, must have at least five years of law enforcement or campaign-finance-enforcement experience, and could serve only one long term. Enforcement cases would move before administrative law judges, the agency could impose civil penalties, issue cease-and-desist orders, issue subpoenas, and audit campaign committees, and it would have to tell the Attorney General to account for how criminal campaign finance cases were being handled.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be ordinary voters and small donors, who rely on timely disclosure of who is funding campaigns and on credible penalties for violations. Candidates and committees that follow the rules would also benefit from clearer advisory opinions, faster public posting of reports, and audits that catch scofflaws rather than leaving them to outlast a deadlocked commission.

how_it_helps.text: The FEC's six seats are split evenly between the two parties, so its decisions often deadlock and enforcement stalls; the bill would replace it with a three-member body in which no two members may have belonged to the same party in the previous five years, and require members to have at least five years of law-enforcement or campaign-finance-enforcement experience and serve only one term [S2][S3].

Enforcement would no longer require a commission vote before anything happens: violations would be tried before administrative law judges, with the agency able to impose civil penalties up to $5,000 per violation ($10,000 or more for knowing and willful violations), issue cease-and-desist orders, and refer criminal violations to the Attorney General [S2][S3].

The agency could conduct audits and field examinations of campaign committees, including random audits of up to 3% of candidate committees a year, and citizens who file sworn complaints would be entitled to a decision, with up to $1,000 of their filing costs reimbursed if a violation is found [S2][S3].

The agency would gain independence from White House control: its budget requests and legislative recommendations could not be pre-cleared by the President or the Office of Management and Budget, and it could litigate in court independently of the Attorney General [S3].

The Comptroller General would have to examine and report to Congress on how the Attorney General enforces the criminal provisions of campaign finance law, and study what funding the new agency needs to do its job [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on campaigns, party committees, and big donors who currently operate in an enforcement environment where violations often go unpunished: they would face real penalties, subpoenas, audits, and in serious cases criminal prosecution. Taxpayers would fund the new agency and its administrative law judges.

drawbacks.text: The bill changes the referee, not the rules: it does not alter contribution limits, disclosure requirements, or outside-spending rules, so critics would say it spends federal money reorganizing an agency without touching the underlying campaign finance laws [S2][S3].

The design carries its own risks: a three-member body with strict party-diversity requirements could still be paralyzed by a single vacancy or one recalcitrant member, the Chair would hold subpoena and staffing power that could concentrate authority in one person, and people who rely in good faith on agency advisory opinions and rules would be shielded from penalties [S3].

Complaints could no longer be anonymous — they must be signed, sworn, notarized, and filed under penalty of perjury — which would raise the bar for citizens and watchdog groups hoping to trigger enforcement, and only $1,000 of their costs would be reimbursable [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — swapping a commission famous for 3-3 party deadlocks for a small, professional, one-term enforcement body with real adjudication and audit powers — addresses a genuine, well-documented weakness in federal campaign finance enforcement, and would cost taxpayers relatively little compared with the sums at stake in federal elections. The honest tradeoffs are that it reorganizes enforcement without changing any substantive rules, concentrates significant power in its chair, and makes citizen complaints harder to file anonymously.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Committee on House Administration, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Shays of Connecticut introduced the bill with Rep. Martin Meehan on June 22, 2006 [S1][S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed [S5][S1].
The bill had one cosponsor and never advanced in the Senate, and the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, killing the bill [S4][S1][S5].

Shays and Meehan were the House's leading campaign finance reformers, best known for the 2002 Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act, and this bill was their follow-on attempt to fix the agency that enforces those laws; similar proposals to restructure the FEC have repeatedly stalled in Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent officeholders and the campaign committees, parties, and large donors who benefit from the existing FEC's slow, deadlock-prone enforcement are better off, because the enforcement system they operate under was left untouched.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican lead sponsor with one Democratic cosponsor — but with only two members behind it, no committee action, and no roll-call votes, the record shows no party-line fight to measure.

industries.industry: Campaign committees and political party organizations
industries.note: The bill would have subjected campaigns and party committees to faster enforcement, administrative law judge proceedings, civil penalties, and random audits of up to 3% of candidate committees a year. Their interest in the bill ran against the public's, since weaker enforcement lets violations go unpunished.

Donors who push the limits of campaign finance law rely on an enforcement agency that often deadlocks; the bill's higher penalties for knowing and willful violations and its referral of criminal cases would have raised their exposure.

industries.industry: FEC commissioners and campaign finance lawyers/consultants
industries.note: The bill would have removed sitting commissioners from office six months after enactment and barred former commissioners from the new agency, while campaign finance lawyers would face a new body with new procedures, advisory opinion deadlines, and reliance rules.
